lead: In the first reading God calls Moses out of a burning bush and sends him to deliver his people: God has seen their misery and will be with Moses. In the Gospel Jesus thanks his Father for hiding these things from the wise and revealing them to infants, and tells of the knowledge that only the Father and the Son share. Both readings show a God who comes down to the lowly. He reveals himself to a shepherd in a wilderness and to the little ones of Galilee. Today the Church also remembers St Camillus de Lellis (died 1614), founder of the Ministers of the Sick; the weekday readings are kept.

r.h: The bush that was not consumed
set: Moses, rescued as a baby and raised in Pharaoh’s house, fled to Midian after killing the Egyptian (2:11–15). There he married Zipporah, the daughter of the priest of Midian, and became a shepherd for his father-in-law. The call at the bush comes in the middle of ordinary work. The Lectionary leaves out vv. 7–8, in which God says he has seen the misery of his people and has come down to deliver them; v. 9 repeats the same message.
str: vv. 1–3: Moses leads the flock to Horeb and sees a bush burning that is not consumed.
vv. 4–6: God calls him by name, tells him to take off his sandals, and says who he is.
vv. 9–10: God has heard Israel’s cry and sends Moses to Pharaoh.
vv. 11–12: Moses objects, “Who am I?”, and God answers, “I will be with you.”
kw: A thorn bush of the desert. Many scholars see a play on the name Sinai, the mountain where Israel will later worship (v. 12).
What belongs to God and is set apart from ordinary use. The ground is holy not because of the place but because God is present there.
The verb is the same as in the divine name of v. 14. God does not answer “Who am I?” with a list of Moses’ gifts. He answers with his own presence.
vv: the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.
Fire in the Bible is a sign of God’s presence (Genesis 15:17; Exodus 19:18). A fire that burns without destroying shows a God who is near, yet does not consume those who come before him.
God called to him out of the bush, “Moses, Moses!” And he said, “Here I am.”
God calls by name, and the answer is the answer of every prophet: hinnēnî, “Here I am”. It is the readiness of Abraham (Genesis 22:1) and of Samuel (1 Samuel 3:4).
Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.
The one who comes near God does so with reverence. Joshua will be told the same near Jericho (Joshua 5:15). Holiness is not frightening for those who come as invited.
The cry of the Israelites has now come to me;
God is not far from suffering. He hears the cry of the enslaved, and he chooses a human being to carry out his rescue.
Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh
The humility of Moses is real. God does not argue it away. He gives the one promise that is enough: “I will be with you” (v. 12).
ch: The Church sees in this scene a revelation of God’s holiness and nearness. The Catechism teaches that before the burning bush Moses learns that God is the Holy One, and it speaks of the prayer of Moses that begins here (CCC 205; 2575). Jesus himself uses the words of v. 6 when he teaches the resurrection: God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Mark 12:26–27). Early Christian writers, including St Gregory of Nyssa (in substance), saw in the bush that burned without being consumed a figure of the Virgin Mary, who carried the divine fire of the Word in her womb and remained a virgin; this reading is still honored in the liturgical hymns of the East and the West.

set: The prayer of Jesus follows his warning to the towns that did not repent (11:20–24). At such a hard moment he does not complain; he gives thanks. He prays in the same chapter where John the Baptist’s doubts and Galilee’s hardness of heart have been described. The prayer is short, but scholars often call it the “Johannine thunderbolt” in the Synoptic Gospels, because it speaks of the Father and the Son with the language we know best from the Gospel of John.
str: v. 25: Jesus thanks the Father who hides these things from the wise and reveals them to infants.
v. 26: “Yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.”
v. 27: all things have been handed over to the Son; the Father and the Son know each other, and the Son reveals the Father to whom he chooses.
kw: The word means to acknowledge openly. It is the praise of the psalms, a confession of what God has done.
Babies, the little ones who cannot speak. In Matthew these are the humble disciples, the ones who need God and know it. The “wise and intelligent” are those who trust their own wisdom.
God’s good pleasure. The mysteries of the kingdom are given not because of human cleverness but because the Father chooses to give them.
vv: you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants;
Jesus does not despise learning; the learned are warned only when learning becomes pride. The Gospel is given to anyone with a humble and open heart.
for such was your gracious will.
Jesus accepts the Father’s way. Revelation is the Father’s gift, and he gives it as he chooses.
no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son
The Son and the Father know each other completely. This is the heart of Jesus’ identity: he is not one prophet among others but the Son who alone can show us the Father.
ch: The Catechism quotes v. 27 to teach that Jesus revealed God as Father in an unheard-of sense, eternally Father in relation to his only Son (CCC 240). It also points to this prayer as the model of Jesus’ own thanksgiving to the Father (CCC 2603). The Church’s great teachers have often pointed to the “little ones” of this passage. St Thérèse of Lisieux, a Doctor of the Church, built her “little way” on the same trust: that God gives himself to the small and humble.

qa: Does Jesus say that education and learning are bad?

No. Jesus does not blame the wise and the intelligent for being learned; he warns against a pride that thinks it needs no one. The Church has always honored learning: many of its saints, such as Augustine, Thomas Aquinas and Edith Stein, were great scholars who approached God as little children.
study: God called Moses in the middle of his ordinary work. Where might God be calling me in the middle of mine?
Jesus rejoices that God reveals himself to the little ones. What would it mean for me to be “small” before God this week?
